excerpt: Gboard Kurukuru Version is Google Japan's conveyor-belt keyboard: 116 keys on four moving belts. Not for sale; build files are free on GitHub.
content:
Gboard Kurukuru Version is a keyboard whose keys move instead of your hands. Four conveyor belts each carry 29 keys, 116 in all, and roll them past your fingers, so you wait for the character you want and press it as it arrives. Upper and lower case letters are both on the belts, which means one hand can type everything and the other stays free for a mouse or, as Google Japan puts it, a cup of tea. Kurukuru is Japanese for going round and round; the GitHub repository calls it the Gboard Conveyor Belt Version.

It is the 15th of the joke-but-buildable keyboards that Google Japan's Gboard team releases every 1 October, following earlier ones such as the Yunomi (teacup) version in 2021, the Bar version in 2022 and the Dial version in 2025. It is not for sale and the repository says it is not an official Google product. Instead, Google published 3D-printable STL files, KiCad board files, firmware and a build guide in the google/mozc-devices repository under the Apache 2.0 licence. The guide covers a motorised Moving Keys Edition built from 157 printed parts, an N20 gear motor, an ATOMS3 Lite controller and 116 Kailh Choc low-profile switches with blank keycaps; a Bluetooth edition that works as a keyboard is listed as coming soon.

The launch was posted on Product Hunt under Google's product page by hunter Zac Zuo on 11 October 2026, and finished #10 for the day with 95 upvotes.

We have not built or tested the Kurukuru Version ourselves. This page brings together Google Japan's announcement, the official GitHub repository and build guide, and the Product Hunt launch, and says where each fact comes from.

paragraphs: Zac Zuo, who posted the launch on Product Hunt, described the Kurukuru Version as the latest in Google Japan's yearly run of deliberately odd keyboards, the 15th after a one-key Morse keyboard, a teacup, a rotary phone and a hat.

He explained the name as the Japanese sound of something going round and round, which is what the keys do: four belts of 29 keys bring each letter to your fingers, and one hand is enough. He pointed builders to the guide for the 3D-printed frame, N20 motor and Choc low-profile switches, with board files and firmware in the same repository, and noted that the keycaps in the parts list are blank, so the legends are up to you.

pricing.intro: Google does not sell the Kurukuru Version. The design files, firmware and build guide are free on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 licence; builders pay only for their own parts and printing.
notes: The build guide lists 157 3D-printed parts, an N20 6V gear motor, a DRV8833 motor driver, an ATOMS3 Lite controller and 116 Kailh Choc V1 switches and keycaps.
The board documentation and the Bluetooth Connection Edition are marked as coming soon in the guide.

alternatives.intro: Nothing else on sale works like this. The nearest options are Google's own Gboard app and the earlier keyboards in the same open-source series, all from Google's official pages.

faq.a: A DIY keyboard from Google Japan's Gboard team in which 116 keys ride on four conveyor belts and come to your fingers, so one hand can type every character.
No. It is not for sale, and the repository says it is not an official Google product. You can build one from the free files on GitHub.

faq.q: What do I need to build one?
faq.a: A 3D printer for 157 parts, plus an N20 gear motor, a DRV8833 motor driver, an ATOMS3 Lite controller, bearings, shafts and screws, and 116 Kailh Choc V1 switches with keycaps, as listed in the build guide.

faq.q: Does the build work as a real keyboard?
faq.a: The published guide covers the Moving Keys Edition, in which the motorised belts circulate. A Bluetooth Connection Edition, described as a functional Bluetooth keyboard, is listed as coming soon.

faq.q: What licence are the files under?
faq.a: The google/mozc-devices repository is published under the Apache License 2.0.
It is the Japanese sound of something going round and round, describing the circulating keys.
